For seafood on Koh Samui, head to Bang Por and Maenam on the north coast, the beach restaurants of Bang Rak, Taling Ngam in the south-west (home of Baan Suan Lung Khai, a MICHELIN Bib Gourmand for 2026, reservation required) or the Lamai Seafood Market (daily about 17:00–24:00). Expect 300–500 THB per person at a local seafood restaurant. Seafood is usually sold by weight from a display on ice, so check whether the price is per kilo or per 100 g, and agree the total, before anything goes on the grill.

Samui is an island of fishing villages, and the best seafood is still cooked within sight of the boats that land it. The catch is squid, blue crab, mackerel, grouper, sea bass, prawns and shellfish from the Gulf of Thailand, cooked in the southern style: hotter, more turmeric and more coconut than in Bangkok. This guide names places verified as listed in 2026 and tells you how to order without nasty surprises on the bill.

Bang Por

Bang Por, at the quiet western end of the north coast past Maenam, is where Samui residents go for a seafood dinner: wooden houses and open-sided pavilions on the sand, fishing boats moored offshore and the sun setting over the sea. The best known is Bang Por Seafood Takho (56/4 Moo 6, Bang Por Beach), listed in the MICHELIN Guide 2026 as "Selected", open daily about 10:00–22:00, at about 300–500 THB per person. Its benchmark dish is pla kapong neung manow, whole sea bass steamed with lime, garlic and chilli, at about 350–500 THB depending on the fish's size. Arrive before 17:30 or book for a sunset table at weekends, and check the displayed prices before you sit down. The beach itself is best for swimming at high tide. See Bang Por.

Maenam

Maenam has two of Samui's MICHELIN-listed southern kitchens. Jun Hom, a 2026 Bib Gourmand, is an open-air beachside restaurant cooking hearty southern dishes to order; its signature is crab curry in coconut milk, and it is open daily about 12:00–20:00. Expect a wait at busy times. Ko Seng (Soi Mae Nam 5, MICHELIN Selected) is a no-frills restaurant over 50 years old, open daily about 10:00–20:00, known for its southern yellow curry. Both close early, so go for lunch or an early dinner. See Maenam.

Bang Rak (Big Buddha Beach)

A strip of beach-front restaurants near the Big Buddha pier displays the day's catch on ice and cooks it to order, with tables on the sand looking across to Koh Phangan. Typical 2026 prices: whole grilled fish 300–500 THB, tiger prawns 300–400 THB, steamed blue crab 250–350 THB and a large Chang beer 60–70 THB. Planes fly low over the bay on their approach to the airport, and the beach is not one for swimming, but the food and the evening light are good. See Big Buddha Beach.

Taling Ngam and Thong Krut

Baan Suan Lung Khai in Taling Ngam, Samui's 2026 MICHELIN Bib Gourmand on the west coast, is a garden house on a coconut plantation serving southern Thai seafood set menus built on the local catch, including blue crab and grilled prawns. It opens daily 11:00–14:00 and 16:30–19:00 and takes reservations only, so call ahead; it is not a walk-in restaurant. It is 30–40 minutes from Chaweng. Taling Ngam faces the Five Islands and has the island's best sunsets; our private longtail cruise to the Five Islands with a Thai seafood dinner on the beach costs 7,500 THB for two. Thong Krut, the fishing village further south, is where our Pig Island boats leave. See Taling Ngam and Thong Krut.

Lamai and Chaweng

The Lamai Seafood Market, which replaced the old Lamai Night Plaza in central Lamai near McDonald's, runs daily from about 17:00 to midnight: pick from the stalls and eat at shared tables. On the ring road south of Lamai, near the Hin Ta and Hin Yai rocks, Sabeinglae is a long-running seafood restaurant open daily about 10:00–22:00, at about 300–500 THB per person; try the mussels baked with glass noodles and ginger. In Chaweng, the walking-street grills from Thursday to Saturday are cheap and cheerful. Be wary of the brightly lit seafood-tank restaurants on Chaweng Beach Road: prices are high, the fish may have been in the tank a while, and touts work the pavement outside. See Lamai and walking streets.

Hua Thanon fish market

Hua Thanon, just south of Lamai, is a Muslim fishing village with Samui's most authentic fish market (open about 07:00–18:00). Go early: the best of the night's catch is sold by mid-morning, when you can watch the boats and the trading. Prices are negotiable for raw fish, and the surrounding stalls sell southern and Thai-Muslim breakfast dishes such as roti and curry. Some cooked-food stalls nearby may cook fish you buy for a fee; ask first, as it isn't a set service. [check] If you're self-catering in a villa, the market is the place to buy, and the Makro wholesale store in Bophut has a fish counter too. See Hua Thanon.

How to order seafood without overpaying

  1. Ask how it's priced: per kilo, per 100 g (khit pen kheet, "by the hundred grams") or per piece. A board that says "100" may mean per 100 g, which is 1,000 THB a kilo.
  2. Watch it weighed: ask to see the scale and the weight, and agree the total before it goes to the kitchen.
  3. Choose the cooking style: grilled (pao), steamed with lime (neung manow), deep-fried with garlic (tod kratiem), or in curry. Ask whether the cooking style costs extra.
  4. Check for set menus: some restaurants sell fixed seafood platters for two, which avoids weighing altogether.
  5. Read the bill: check for dishes you didn't order and for service charges or "++" (10 % service and 7 % VAT) that weren't on the menu.
  6. Pay sensibly: most seafood restaurants take cards; always pay in THB and decline any offer to charge in your home currency.

Samui seafood dishes to try

  • Wai khua: octopus simmered in coconut milk, Samui's signature dish.
  • Gaeng poo bai cha plu: crab curry with wild betel leaves and coconut milk, served with rice noodles.
  • Pla kapong neung manow: whole sea bass steamed in a lime, garlic and chilli broth.
  • Goong pao: grilled prawns with spicy seafood dipping sauce; 80–120 THB a portion at markets.
  • Pla muek yang: grilled squid, a market staple.
  • Hoy mang poo ob woon sen: mussels baked with glass noodles and ginger.
  • Gaeng som / gaeng lueang pla: the southern sour yellow curry with fish, fiercely hot and turmeric-yellow.
  • Tod man pla: fried fish cakes with cucumber relish.

More southern dishes and how to order spice levels: Koh Samui restaurants.

Lobster and large grouper are priced by weight and can cost several thousand baht; always confirm the weight and total first. Resort seafood restaurants add "++".

Sustainability

  • Skip shark fin and anything sold as turtle or wild-caught reef fish of unusual size.
  • Ask what is local and in season; squid, mackerel and blue crab are the everyday Gulf catch.
  • Avoid juvenile crabs and egg-carrying females, which some restaurants still sell.
  • Don't buy coral, shells or dried seahorses as souvenirs.

Allergies and food safety

  • Allergies: fish sauce, shrimp paste and oyster sauce are in most Thai dishes, not just seafood. Carry a card in Thai: "phom/chan pae ahaan talay" means "I'm allergic to seafood".
  • Freshness: eat where the turnover is high, the fish has clear eyes and the display is on plenty of ice.
  • Shellfish: be more careful with mussels, clams and oysters in the hot months; skip them if you have any doubt.
  • Ice and water: tube ice with a hole is factory-made and safe; drink sealed bottled water.
  • If you get ill: pharmacies sell rehydration salts; see pharmacies and hospitals.

Seafood with a boat trip

Some of the best seafood on Samui comes with a day on the water. The Pig Island sunset tour (1,550 THB adult, 1,350 THB child) includes dinner and runs every day of the year from Thong Krut. On the Thai fishing boat day trip from Big Buddha pier (1,800 THB adult) your catch is cooked on board, and the private longtail to Pig Island (5,950 THB per boat) can stop for lunch in a fishing village. Hotel pickup is included from most areas of Koh Samui.
